AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) has a reported incidence of 1.9 - 4.3%. Disease progression is associated with surgery, with most studies focusing on OPLL progression following laminoplasty. It is believed the continued range of motion following surgery places strain on adjacent levels, driving calcification of the ligament. We present a case of marked progression of OPLL at levels adjacent to a previous anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF).

AbstractText.Label: CASE REPORT
AbstractText.content: A 59-year-old male initially presented for progressive loss of balance and dexterity, and underwent a C4-6 ACDF procedure. One-year postoperative CT imaging showed fusion across C4-6 with no evidence of OPLL at any level. Two years following index surgery, the patient reported right-side arm pain. CT imaging revealed new minimal OPLL opposite the C3-4 level that was not causing cord compression. A sparing midline bilateral C3-7 laminotomy was performed to correct stenosis observed by MRI. Seven years following the index procedure, the patient presented with myelopathic symptoms exceeding his index presentation. CT imaging revealed marked progression of the OPLL. Patient underwent a C2-T2 posterior fusion with laminectomy from C2-C7 and responded well with gradual improvements in balance and arm pain following surgery.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: While largely studied following laminoplasty, our report demonstrates that OPLL progression may similarly occur following ACDF and supports the concept of motion-related OPLL progression.
